sourceNotes: Seeded from MCS roleplay performance indicators and marketing cluster exam data.
Drawn in three tiers: MCS event flavor, then this event's own instructional areas, then the rest of the marketing cluster exam blueprint.
Terms are scoped for future vocab-card, quiz, and event-filter UI use.

terms.definition: Price per thousand impressions that actually rendered in view, so it is computed as the served CPM divided by the viewability rate — a $10 CPM delivered at 50% viewability really costs $20 per thousand seen.
terms.whyItMatters: A media-buying roleplay that asks which of two display placements is cheaper is decided on this number, not the quoted rate: the cheaper served CPM loses once its viewability rate is applied.

terms.definition: Revenue or spend restated onto a per-thousand-impressions basis — earnings divided by impressions, times 1,000 — so a CPC, CPA or flat-fee buy can be compared against a CPM buy on one scale. $300 on 200,000 impressions is a $1.50 eCPM.
terms.whyItMatters: When a client hands you a mixed plan of CPC search, CPA affiliate and CPM display and asks which line to cut, converting all three to eCPM is the only way to rank them in a presentation.

terms.definition: Video spend divided by the number of plays that reached 100% completion, which prices only finished views — unlike cost per view, where a platform may bill at 30 seconds or at the end of a shorter ad, so the two metrics can differ several-fold on the same flight.
terms.whyItMatters: A pre-roll buy judged on CPV can look efficient while most viewers skip; the exam question that asks why a video campaign with a low CPV delivered no message recall is answered with completion rate and CPCV.

terms.definition: The counting threshold an impression must clear to be billed as seen: at least 50% of the ad's pixels in the viewport for at least one continuous second for display, and 50% of pixels for two continuous seconds for video, with large-format units allowed 30% of pixels for one second.
terms.whyItMatters: In a roleplay where a publisher and an agency argue over an invoice, quoting the pixel-and-duration threshold decides which impressions are billable rather than leaving it to opinion.

terms.definition: Gap between the publisher's impression count and the agency's third-party ad server count, caused by latency, blocked tags and count-on-request versus count-on-render logic; roughly 10% is the accepted tolerance, and inside it the buy is reconciled and billed on the third-party number.
terms.whyItMatters: A trafficking question that gives two impression totals is testing whether you know the 10% tolerance and which count pays; above it the advertiser withholds and asks for an investigation or a makegood.

terms.definition: The lookback period inside which a conversion is still credited to a prior ad click or view — commonly 7 days after a click and 1 day after a view. Lengthening it moves conversions into the campaign and lowers reported cost per acquisition without a dollar of spend changing.
terms.whyItMatters: When a client claims a channel's CPA improved month over month, the first thing to check in a presentation is whether the window was widened; the exam tests that the metric moved, not the media.

terms.definition: A U-shaped credit split that assigns 40% of a conversion's value to the first touch, 40% to the last touch and divides the remaining 20% across every middle touch — deliberately rewarding the channel that created awareness as well as the one that closed.
terms.whyItMatters: Awareness media always looks worthless under last-click reporting; recommending this split with its 40/20/40 weights is how a competitor defends an upper-funnel line item in a budget roleplay.

terms.definition: Credit weighted by recency on an exponential curve, typically a seven-day half-life: a touchpoint one week before the conversion earns half the credit of one on the conversion day, and two weeks out a quarter of it.
terms.whyItMatters: For a long consideration purchase, choosing between this model and a U-shaped split changes which channel the budget follows — a standard media-planning defense in a Marketing Communications roleplay.

terms.definition: The average number of people tuned to a station for at least five minutes within a given 15-minute block; dividing it by the market population and multiplying by 100 yields the AQH rating, which is the rating point a radio buy is actually priced against.
terms.whyItMatters: Radio schedules are costed as cost per point, and the point comes from this five-minute rule — a broadcast buying question is unsolvable without converting AQH persons into an AQH rating first.

terms.definition: The count of different people who tuned in for at least five minutes anywhere in a daypart, each counted once no matter how often they returned — so it measures reach, and dividing it by average quarter-hour persons gives turnover, the number of audiences the station cycles through.
terms.whyItMatters: A station selling on a big cume and a buyer costing the schedule on AQH are quoting two different numbers; the exam asks which one supports a reach goal and which one supports frequency.

terms.definition: Total exposures a schedule delivers with duplication left in — gross rating points times the universe divided by 100 — so the figure always exceeds net reach, and reach times average frequency reproduces it exactly.
terms.whyItMatters: Given GRPs and a market population, this conversion is the single most common media-math item on a marketing communications exam, and it is also how a plan is restated for a client who thinks in people, not points.

terms.definition: The share of a vehicle's audience that falls in the target divided by that group's share of the general population, times 100 — 100 is parity, 120 means the vehicle over-delivers the target by 20%, and below 100 the buy is paying for waste.
terms.whyItMatters: Choosing between two magazines with similar CPMs comes down to this index, and a competitor who cannot say what an index of 85 means will recommend the cheaper, wronger book.

terms.definition: The out-of-home audience figure for a single unit — the average number of people per day passing it with a reasonable opportunity to see the face — and it is the denominator that turns a panel's monthly rate into a comparable CPM.
terms.whyItMatters: An outdoor proposal quotes a flat monthly price per board; converting each board to a CPM through this circulation figure is the only way to rank locations in a media-buying roleplay.

terms.definition: The out-of-home weight level named for the share of the market it covers daily: a #50 showing buys enough faces to deliver daily impressions equal to 50% of the market population, a #100 delivers 100%, and the number is a daily GRP level rather than a count of boards.
terms.whyItMatters: A vendor who quotes '25 posters' has told you nothing; asking for the showing level converts the offer into daily GRPs your plan can be held to, which is exactly what a judge listens for.

terms.definition: A print comparison figure computed as the cost of one agate line multiplied by 1,000,000 and divided by circulation, which restates newspapers of wildly different sizes as one price per line per million readers.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked to justify buying the smaller paper, a competitor who shows a lower milline rate has proved the cheaper audience; comparing raw line rates between papers proves nothing.

terms.definition: The circulation or impression figure a publisher contractually guarantees and is independently audited against; missing it obliges the publisher to rebate the advertiser or supply replacement weight, and rates are set on the guarantee rather than on actual delivery.
terms.whyItMatters: When a magazine's audited circulation comes in under the guarantee, knowing the remedy is a rebate or a makegood is what turns an advertiser's complaint into a settled negotiation in a roleplay.

terms.definition: Replacement weight supplied free when a schedule under-delivers its guaranteed rating points or impressions, or when a unit runs wrong — settled in equivalent audience delivery in a comparable daypart, not in a cash refund of the dollars spent.
terms.whyItMatters: A station that delivers 180 of 200 guaranteed GRPs owes the missing 20 points, and the roleplay tests whether you negotiate the replacement in equivalent audience rather than accepting cheap late-night filler.

terms.definition: The traditional media compensation of 15% of gross billing retained by the agency, so the net cost owed the medium is the gross times 0.85 — and grossing a net price back up requires multiplying by 1.1765, because 15% of gross equals 17.65% of net.
terms.whyItMatters: A quoted net rate and a quoted gross rate for the same spot differ by that 17.65% markup; a budget question that mixes the two is unsolvable unless you convert, and clients notice which way you rounded.

terms.definition: The federal rule entitling a legally qualified candidate to a station's cheapest rate for the same class and time period, during the 45 days before a primary and the 60 days before a general election, regardless of the volume any commercial advertiser bought to earn that rate.
terms.whyItMatters: It explains why commercial inventory gets preempted and repriced every fall election season — a scheduling conflict a competitor must be able to explain to a client whose flight lands inside the window.

terms.definition: Federal requirement that a commercial not be transmitted louder than the program it accompanies, enforced not by opinion but by measured average loudness under the ATSC A/85 recommended practice, whose United States target is roughly -24 LKFS.
terms.whyItMatters: A spot rejected at station QC for loudness is a production problem with a numeric fix, and knowing the target keeps a Marketing Communications competitor from promising a client a re-edit that will fail again.

terms.definition: Statutory caps on commercial matter inside programming aimed at children 12 and under — 10.5 minutes per hour on weekends and 12 minutes per hour on weekdays — enforced alongside bans on host-selling and on program-length commercials.
terms.whyItMatters: A client wanting to advertise a toy inside a kids block is constrained by these per-hour minutes and by who may deliver the message, and an ethics-flavored exam item turns on the exact figures.

terms.definition: A private federal suit under Section 43(a) letting one competitor sue another over false or misleading commercial advertising, requiring a false or misleading statement of fact in interstate commerce, deception that is material to purchase, and resulting injury — with injunctions, the defendant's profits and damages available, and no FTC involvement at all.
terms.whyItMatters: When a rival's comparative ad misstates your client's product, the answer is not to file with the FTC but to name this claim and its elements — a distinction that separates a prepared roleplay from a vague one.

terms.definition: The evidentiary bar an objective advertising claim must meet — tests or studies run by qualified people using procedures generally accepted in the field, typically at least one well-controlled randomized human clinical trial for a health claim — and it has to exist before the ad runs, not be assembled after a challenge.
terms.whyItMatters: A client who wants 'clinically proven' in the headline is asking for a claim that needs this file on hand at launch; explaining the prior-substantiation timing is the professional answer in an ethics roleplay.

terms.definition: The FTC standard for qualifying information: unavoidable, delivered in the same medium as the claim it modifies, placed close to that claim, and worded so an ordinary consumer understands it — a hyperlink, a hashtag, or fine print past the fold does not satisfy it.
terms.whyItMatters: Influencer and native placements live or die on this test, so a competitor briefing a creator has to say where the disclosure goes, not merely that one is required.

terms.definition: A scheduling philosophy that spreads weight into continuous weekly presence chasing one-plus weekly reach, instead of concentrating a burst to build three-plus frequency, on the reasoning that the exposure nearest a purchase decision does the persuading.
terms.whyItMatters: It is the argument for turning a client's four-week blitz into a year of light weekly coverage, and a judge expects the reach-versus-frequency trade to be named out loud.

terms.definition: The binding contract behind a media buy, specifying flight dates, units, placements, rates, targeting, the delivery guarantee and the cancellation terms — it is the document a delivery dispute is settled against, and verbal confirmations are not.
terms.whyItMatters: When a publisher under-delivers, the remedy comes from this paperwork, so a roleplay about a shorted campaign is really a question about what the buyer wrote down before the flight started.

terms.definition: Planning shorthand for average frequency — total exposures divided by net reach — counting chances to encounter the message rather than proven attention, which is why it is an upper bound on what the audience really absorbed.
terms.whyItMatters: A plan promising a client four OTS is promising exposures, not four people persuaded; distinguishing the two protects a competitor from over-claiming in a presentation.

terms.definition: Communication that informs, persuades, and reminds customers about offerings.
terms.whyItMatters: Promotion choices must fit the audience, message, and budget.

terms.definition: Raw, unprocessed facts and figures collected through observation, measurement, or research.
terms.whyItMatters: All information management begins with knowing what counts as reliable data.

terms.definition: The activities a business uses to build satisfaction, trust, and loyalty.
terms.whyItMatters: Strong customer relations support repeat business and reputation.

terms.definition: The ability to understand and manage emotions in yourself and others.
terms.whyItMatters: It underlies teamwork, service, and conflict-resolution answers.

terms.definition: The overall approach a business uses to reach customers and meet marketing goals.
terms.whyItMatters: Case studies require strategies that fit business objectives and market conditions.

terms.definition: The process of creating, communicating, and delivering value to customers.
terms.whyItMatters: This is the umbrella concept behind many cluster and roleplay decisions.

terms.definition: Planning, developing, marketing, and managing offerings across their life.
terms.whyItMatters: It ensures offerings meet customer needs and generate sustainable revenue.

terms.definition: Reach multiplied by average frequency, the one number that sizes a schedule's total weight: 40% of the target seen four times is 160. The same 160 can be bought as 80% reach at 2.0 frequency, which is why the figure alone never describes a schedule.
terms.whyItMatters: Media-planning items hand the competitor a reach figure and a frequency figure and ask for the schedule's weight, or give the weight and one factor and ask for the other; a roleplay defending a media plan to a client is expected to state both halves, not just the total.

terms.definition: Reached only when a table already satisfies first normal form, which removes repeating groups so each cell holds one value, and second normal form, which removes any non-key column depending on just part of a composite key, and then additionally removes transitive dependency — a non-key column determined by another non-key column rather than by the key.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam table showing a customer's ZIP code alongside the city that ZIP code determines is the classic normalization item, and the tested answer names which form that violation breaks.

terms.definition: The total profit a business expects from a customer over the whole relationship.
terms.whyItMatters: CLV guides how much to invest in retention and service.

terms.term: Goleman's four-domain model of emotional intelligence
terms.definition: Sorts emotional competence into four domains — self-awareness, self-management, social awareness, relationship management — arranged as a 2x2 grid: the left column is personal competence (handling yourself), the right column is social competence (handling others), the top row is recognition and the bottom row is regulation. It is a mixed model of learnable workplace competencies, so it is assessed with a 360-degree rater inventory rather than with a right-answer test.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam item that lists four manager behaviors and asks which one is social awareness rather than relationship management is scored against this grid, and a management roleplay judge expects a candidate to name which domain a weakness sits in before proposing the fix.

terms.definition: The ceiling on category demand in a defined area and period — every possible buyer times the maximum quantity each could buy times unit price; one firm's share of that ceiling is sales potential, and the volume it actually expects to sell on the funded budget is the sales forecast.
terms.whyItMatters: Sizing items on the marketing exam hand you a population, a purchase rate and a price and expect the whole-industry ceiling, not one company's number; in a market-identification roleplay the judge is listening for the three-step narrowing said in order.

terms.definition: Value created by converting raw materials into a finished good a buyer actually wants — wheat into bread, bauxite into a can — as distinct from place utility (moving the good to where the buyer shops), time utility (having it on hand at the hour demand occurs), and possession utility (transferring ownership through payment terms); a redesign adds form utility, a faster truck does not.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays that ask how marketing adds value to a product are scored on naming which of the four utilities each activity creates and separating them; a general answer about 'adding value' loses the point.

terms.definition: Counts how many separate product lines a company carries, never how many items sit inside them: a grocer running dairy, bakery, and frozen lines has a width of 3 even when those lines hold 400 items between them, while product mix depth counts the items within one line.
terms.whyItMatters: A mix-planning roleplay that asks how a retailer should expand expects width and depth reported as two different counts; answering with adjectives like 'broad' instead of a number loses the indicator.

terms.definition: The blend of advertising, publicity, sales promotion, and personal selling.
terms.whyItMatters: A mix lets competitors recommend more than one communication path.

terms.definition: An organized, computer-managed collection of related data that can be stored and retrieved systematically.
terms.whyItMatters: Businesses run everything from inventory to customer records on databases.

terms.definition: A relationship of mutual understanding and trust between a business and its customers.
terms.whyItMatters: Building rapport raises trust and the odds of repeat business.

terms.definition: A situation where two or more moral principles conflict and demand judgment.
terms.whyItMatters: Recognizing and resolving dilemmas is central to leadership and compliance.

terms.definition: Discovering and defining the markets where a business can sell its offering.
terms.whyItMatters: Identifying the right market is the foundation of any marketing plan.

terms.definition: Intangible activities that satisfy customer needs and wants.
terms.whyItMatters: Services require different quality, staffing, and marketing choices than goods.

terms.definition: The stages a product passes through: introduction, growth, maturity, and decline.
terms.whyItMatters: The stage a product is in drives its marketing, pricing, and distribution.

terms.definition: Rating points counted only against the demographic actually being bought instead of against every household in the market, so a broad-appeal buy delivering 200 gross rating points may deliver just 60 of these if only 30% of its viewers fall inside the target.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam item that shows a schedule looking strong on total weight but thin on the buying demographic is testing this distinction, and a media-plan roleplay that quotes only the gross figure to a client buying an 18-to-34 audience has hidden the waste.

terms.definition: The four guarantees a relational transaction makes — atomicity, meaning all steps commit or none do; consistency, meaning no declared rule is left broken; isolation, meaning concurrent transactions cannot read each other's partial work; and durability, meaning a committed write survives a crash — and precisely the set that BASE-style distributed stores relax in exchange for availability.
terms.whyItMatters: A banking-transfer scenario asks what keeps a debit from posting when the matching credit fails, and the graded answer names atomicity within this set rather than saying the system is careful.

terms.definition: Contacts fully resolved on the first interaction divided by total contacts handled — 1,200 of 1,500 is 80%. A case that is transferred to a second agent or reopened later counts as a failure even if it is solved the same day, which is why it moves in the opposite direction from average handle time whenever agents rush callers off the line.
terms.whyItMatters: In a contact-center roleplay judged on service improvement, the fix a competitor proposes has to raise this number; trimming call length by promising a callback lowers it.

terms.definition: Treats emotional intelligence as a genuine intelligence with four ranked branches — perceiving emotion, using emotion to facilitate thinking, understanding how emotions combine and change, and managing emotion — and measures it with the MSCEIT, a maximum-performance test whose items are scored against consensus or expert norms instead of asking a person to rate themselves.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam questions that contrast the two dominant EI frameworks turn on this: this one is an ability test with scoreable answers, while the competency model is a rated inventory of habits, and picking the wrong one loses the item.

terms.definition: One company's maximum obtainable slice of category demand — market potential multiplied by the highest share it could hold with unlimited marketing effort; it always sits above the sales forecast, which discounts that ceiling down to the effort and budget actually approved.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam questions that give an industry ceiling and a best-case share expect this middle figure, and a competitor who reports it as the forecast overstates the plan's revenue line in front of a judge.

terms.definition: Value added by making ownership transferable — credit terms, layaway, financing, leasing, the transaction mechanics themselves — rather than by making the good (form utility), delivering it to the buyer's location (place utility), or holding it until demand appears (time utility); a dealer that adds 60-month zero-interest financing changes the product's form, place, and time not at all.
terms.whyItMatters: Hospitality and finance roleplays that ask you to justify offering a payment plan want the answer framed as a marketing utility the firm creates, not as a favor to the customer.

terms.definition: Counts the individual items inside a single line -- sizes, flavors, formulations, models: a toothpaste line of 4 flavors in 3 tube sizes is 12 items deep, and adding a fifth flavor deepens the mix without widening it, because width counts lines alone.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items give a table of lines and items and ask for one number; students who add every item in the company report the length instead of the depth of the line asked about.

terms.definition: Paid, nonpersonal communication delivered through media to large audiences.
terms.whyItMatters: Advertising builds broad brand awareness efficiently and at scale.

terms.definition: A warehouse layout placing one central fact table of numeric measures among denormalized dimension tables, each exactly one join away from the facts; the snowflake variant normalizes those dimensions into further sub-tables, which saves storage and removes redundancy but adds a join to every query that touches them.
terms.whyItMatters: A database-design item shows a sales fact table ringed by product, store and date tables and asks why the dimensions repeat values instead of being split further.

terms.definition: Talk time plus hold time plus after-call work, divided by contacts handled — 6 minutes of talk, 1 minute of hold and 3 minutes of wrap-up across 40 calls averages 10 minutes. Leaving wrap-up out of the numerator is the standard error, and it makes every staffing model built on the figure understaff the queue.
terms.whyItMatters: Staffing math in a peak-demand hospitality or call-center roleplay starts here, and exam items expect the wrap-up term to be inside the average.

terms.definition: Emotional self-perception measured as a personality disposition: instruments such as the TEIQue ask a person to agree or disagree with statements about themselves across roughly fifteen facets, so the score records self-belief and overlaps heavily with the Big Five. Ability EI, by contrast, is scored on correct answers to emotion problems, which is why the two kinds of measure correlate only weakly with each other.
terms.whyItMatters: A human resources roleplay in which a candidate proposes an EI screen for hiring is judged on knowing that a self-report inventory can be gamed by an applicant while a performance test cannot.

terms.definition: Sizing demand from the bottom up: identify every potential buyer in each segment or territory, estimate units each would buy, and sum units times price across them. The chain-ratio method runs the opposite direction, starting from a national total and multiplying it down through successive percentages.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-to-business sizing cases on the exam name a count of establishments and a per-establishment purchase rate, which is a buildup problem; using a national percentage chain there produces the wrong answer.

terms.definition: The benefit a customer believes they receive compared with the cost or effort.
terms.whyItMatters: Value helps explain why a customer chooses one offer over another.

terms.definition: A group of related products sold under one brand or category.
terms.whyItMatters: Line decisions balance customer choice against cost and complexity.

terms.definition: One percent of all the households or people in a market's universe, counted whether or not their set is switched on, so a program watched by 90,000 homes in a 1,500,000-household market rates 6.0.
terms.whyItMatters: Cost-per-point math on the marketing exam starts here, and competitors lose the item by treating the figure as a share of viewers rather than a percent of the whole market.

terms.definition: Documents and files that capture a business's transactions, operations, and decisions.
terms.whyItMatters: Accurate records are required for compliance, accountability, and historical reference.

terms.definition: A mindset committed to meeting customer needs and providing quality help.
terms.whyItMatters: It helps employees deliver consistent, customer-focused interactions.

terms.definition: Respecting and adapting to the values and practices of different cultures.
terms.whyItMatters: It lets a business serve diverse markets and build inclusive teams.

terms.definition: The specific customer group a business chooses as its primary marketing audience.
terms.whyItMatters: Recommendations are stronger when they name a specific audience.

terms.definition: Assigns every small geographic unit — a ZIP+4 or a census block group of roughly 100 to 200 households — to a lifestyle cluster by joining census demographics to purchase data, on the assumption that neighbors buy alike; Nielsen's PRIZM sorts U.S. neighborhoods into 68 such clusters, so media and direct mail are bought against a cluster code rather than against an age band.
terms.whyItMatters: Site-selection and direct-mail roleplays reward naming the cluster system and the unit it works at; saying 'we will target that ZIP code' without the cluster logic reads as guessing.

terms.definition: Total number of items across every line the firm sells, equal to width multiplied by average depth: 5 lines averaging 8 items each gives a length of 40, so a company can lengthen its mix without widening it by adding items to lines it already runs.
terms.whyItMatters: Product-mix questions hand you width and average depth and expect the multiplication; a roleplay judge scoring a merchandising plan looks for the total item count you commit the buyer to carrying.

terms.definition: Short-term incentives like coupons, contests, and discounts that spur purchases.
terms.whyItMatters: Promotions drive quick sales, trial, and inventory clearance.

terms.definition: A descriptive attribute that changes over time and forces a documented choice: Type 1 overwrites the old value and loses all history, while Type 2 closes the existing row with an end date and inserts a new version row, so a sale made two years ago still ties to the sales territory that was in force on the day it happened.
terms.whyItMatters: When a roleplay judge asks why last year's totals shifted after a store was reassigned to a new district, the answer is which of these two handling types the warehouse used.

terms.definition: The share of contacts answered inside a stated number of seconds, written as a pair — the industry default target is 80% answered within 20 seconds, and the other 20% may wait any length of time at all. That blind spot is why it is reported alongside average speed of answer rather than instead of it.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay that asks a competitor to set a staffing target for a holiday peak wants this pair of numbers, not a promise to answer quickly.

terms.definition: Maps five ways of handling a disagreement — competing, collaborating, compromising, avoiding and accommodating — on two axes: assertiveness, meaning concern for your own outcome, and cooperativeness, meaning concern for the other party's. Collaborating is high on both and costs the most time; compromising sits at the middle of both and splits the difference, so treating those two as synonyms is the classic wrong answer.
terms.whyItMatters: Conflict roleplays name a deadline, and the judge wants the mode matched to it — collaborate when the relationship and the outcome both matter and time exists, compromise when it does not.

terms.definition: The smoothed yearly rate that carries a starting value to an ending value over n years: (ending value / beginning value)^(1/n) - 1. It deliberately hides year-to-year swings, so a category that jumped 40% and then fell 20% still reports one steady rate.
terms.whyItMatters: Marketing-plan questions that give a market size for two years and a span expect this exponent, not the two values subtracted and divided by the number of years.

terms.definition: Sorts U.S. adults into eight consumer types on two axes — primary motivation (ideals, achievement or self-expression) and level of resources and innovation — with Innovators at the top of the resource axis and Survivors at the bottom; it classifies the individual from a survey instrument, whereas PRIZM classifies the neighborhood from census and purchase data, so the two cannot be used interchangeably.
terms.whyItMatters: When a judge asks which segmentation system you would buy, naming VALS and stating its two axes shows you know the difference between a person-level and a household-level system.

terms.definition: Building a company's overall reputation and identity across its offerings.
terms.whyItMatters: Strong corporate branding creates loyalty and justifies premium pricing.

terms.definition: The percentage of sets actually in use that are tuned to a given program, so a show rating 6 in a market where only half the sets are on carries a 12 — the figure is always larger than the program's own rating because its denominator is smaller.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items pair a rating and this figure for the same program and ask which one a national advertiser should buy against; the answer is the rating, because only it is measured against the full market a campaign is paying to cover.

terms.definition: The person accountable for the day-to-day quality, field definitions and correction of one data domain, executing rules that somebody else sets; the data owner is the business executive who sets those rules, signs off on the definitions and approves who may see the domain — accountability for the policy versus accountability for the practice.
terms.whyItMatters: Records-monitoring roleplays ask who should approve a new customer field and who should fix the 400 records already entered wrong, and the two answers are different roles.

terms.definition: Contacts that disconnect while waiting divided by contacts offered — 90 hang-ups out of 3,000 offered is 3%, and most centers exclude calls dropped inside the first 5 seconds as misdials before reporting it. Under 5% is the common acceptance band, and the number rises non-linearly once average wait passes the caller's patience threshold.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items hand over the offered and abandoned counts and expect both the percentage and the staffing conclusion drawn from it.

terms.definition: Divides what is known about a person into four panes by crossing known-to-self against known-to-others: open, blind, hidden and unknown. Asking for feedback shrinks the blind pane, while voluntary self-disclosure shrinks the hidden pane — the two moves are not interchangeable, and only the first can surface a habit you cannot see in yourself.
terms.whyItMatters: A written item asking which pane a manager reduces by running a 360-degree review, and roleplays that ask a competitor to assess personal strengths and weaknesses, both depend on separating feedback from disclosure.

terms.definition: A written document laying out marketing objectives, strategies, and tactics for a period.
terms.whyItMatters: The plan guides all promotional and customer-facing decisions.

terms.definition: The way customers decide what, when, where, and why to purchase.
terms.whyItMatters: Understanding buying-behavior factors lets competitors target the right message and offer.

terms.definition: Adds a new size, flavor, color, or form under an existing brand inside the category it already competes in; a brand extension instead carries that brand into a different category -- a cherry version of a cola is the first, a cola-branded snack chip is the second.
terms.whyItMatters: Branding roleplays ask you to grow a brand without new advertising weight; naming the wrong one of the pair gives away that you cannot tell same-category growth from category entry.

terms.definition: Direct, person-to-person communication to inform, persuade, and build relationships.
terms.whyItMatters: It enables customized pitches and problem-solving for high-value sales.

terms.definition: The combination of hardware, software, data, and people used to collect, process, store, and share information.
terms.whyItMatters: Understanding systems is key when competitors evaluate technology investments.

terms.definition: The commitment a company makes about the value and experience it will deliver.
terms.whyItMatters: Knowing the promise helps employees deliver a consistent experience.

terms.definition: Techniques to address disagreements and reach mutually acceptable solutions.
terms.whyItMatters: Strong conflict resolution keeps teams cohesive and prevents escalation.

terms.definition: The portion of total addressable demand a firm's product, price point and channels can actually reach — the total narrowed to the segments and geographies it serves. Narrow it once more by the share realistically winnable in the plan period and you have the serviceable obtainable market.
terms.whyItMatters: Written-event plans that state one giant industry figure lose points; judges expect the total narrowed twice, with the reason for each cut named.

terms.definition: A candidate group qualifies as a market segment only if it passes five named tests — measurable (its size and buying power can be quantified), substantial (large and profitable enough to serve alone), accessible (reachable through some channel or medium), differentiable (it responds differently from other segments to a change in the mix) and actionable (the firm can actually build and run a program for it); failing any one of the five makes it a description of people, not a segment.
terms.whyItMatters: Market-planning roleplays that ask you to defend a chosen segment are scored on running it against the criteria out loud; the segment competitors usually pick fails 'substantial' or 'accessible'.

terms.definition: Adds items between price or feature points a line already covers, usually to close a gap a rival occupies -- dropping a $600 model between the existing $450 and $850 units; line stretching instead pushes the line past the top or bottom of its current range.
terms.whyItMatters: A merchandising roleplay that reports a competitor winning a mid-price slot is scored on filling the gap rather than repricing the whole line.

terms.definition: The number of exposures needed inside a single purchase cycle before a message registers at all — below it the spend is wasted and above it the spend is redundant. The working planning standard is three exposures, from Krugman's three-hit theory.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay where a client wants the budget spread over more vehicles is a test of this: adding vehicles raises reach but can drop everyone below three exposures, leaving a campaign that technically touched the market and communicated nothing.

terms.definition: A written table stating how long each class of record is kept and when it must be destroyed, built on statutory floors rather than preference: the IRS's ordinary three-year assessment window, seven years for records supporting a bad-debt or worthless-securities claim, and the Sarbanes-Oxley requirement that audit work papers survive seven years.
terms.whyItMatters: A business-records roleplay asks how long the storeroom keeps signed invoices before shredding them, and a judge expects a statutory minimum, not a guess like 'a few years'.

terms.definition: Total queue wait across all answered contacts divided by the number answered — an arithmetic mean, so it hides the tail. Nine callers waiting 5 seconds and one waiting 300 still reports 34.5 seconds, while the 80/20 service level exposes the outlier because it counts callers rather than averaging them.
terms.whyItMatters: In a service-improvement roleplay, the competitor who explains why the average looks healthy while customers complain is using this against service level.

terms.definition: Reinterpreting a situation until the required feeling is genuinely experienced, so expression and emotion match — as against surface acting, where a smile is layered over an unchanged feeling. The two produce the same visible behavior with opposite costs, because it is the mismatch inside surface acting, not the effort of acting, that drives exhaustion.
terms.whyItMatters: Coaching roleplays where a supervisor must help a frustrated employee face the public are graded on teaching the employee to reframe the customer's motive rather than just ordering a better face.

terms.definition: The slice of the serviceable available market a company expects to capture within the plan horizon: SAM times a realistic share percentage, so a $200 million SAM at 4% share is an $8 million target. Unlike SAM it is a forecast the plan is held to, not a ceiling.
terms.whyItMatters: This is the number a judge compares against the plan's revenue projection and marketing budget; a SOM larger than the funded plan can deliver is the fastest way to lose credibility in a presentation.

terms.definition: The blend of product, price, place, and promotion used to reach a target market.
terms.whyItMatters: The four Ps are the standard framework for building a marketing recommendation.

terms.definition: How a product is differentiated in the market and in customers' minds.
terms.whyItMatters: Clear positioning conveys unique value and targets the right segments.

terms.definition: Activities that build positive relationships with the public and media.
terms.whyItMatters: PR manages image, trust, and credibility through third-party voices.

terms.definition: An instruction that suspends the retention schedule and freezes every document touching anticipated or filed litigation, overriding routine destruction until counsel lifts it; skipping it exposes the company to spoliation sanctions under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 37(e) even when the deletion was only the ordinary schedule running as designed.
terms.whyItMatters: In a legal-issues roleplay where a customer has threatened suit, the first correct action is stopping automatic email deletion — not gathering documents after the subpoena arrives.

terms.definition: The actions a business takes to fix a poor experience and restore trust.
terms.whyItMatters: Recovery answers the complaint and negative-feedback scenarios competitors face.

terms.definition: Reinterpreting a situation before the emotion peaks so that the feeling itself changes — an antecedent-focused move, as opposed to expressive suppression, which lets the feeling run and hides only the outward signal. Suppression is the costlier of the pair: it consumes attention, degrades memory of the conversation, and leaves internal arousal untouched.
terms.whyItMatters: An item asking which self-control tactic preserves a manager's recall of a hostile meeting expects reappraisal, and roleplays on composure reward reframing over a clenched poker face.

terms.definition: An assessment of internal and external factors affecting a business's marketing.
terms.whyItMatters: Understanding the situation must come before any recommendation.

terms.definition: Empirical pattern in which roughly the top 20% of a category's buyers generate about 80% of its volume, and the heavier half of buyers accounts for 80% to 90% of units in many packaged-goods categories — so a 10% lift among heavy users is worth several times the same percentage lift among light users, and a promotion measured in customers reached can be worth less than one measured in volume reached.
terms.whyItMatters: Promotion-budget roleplays that ask where to spend a limited fund are won by weighting the target by consumption share rather than by headcount.

terms.definition: Extends a line beyond the price range it now serves -- downward into cheaper segments, upward into premium ones, or both at once, as when a marque starting at $30,000 adds a $19,000 entry car; line filling by contrast stays entirely inside the range already covered.
terms.whyItMatters: Positioning roleplays warn about trading down: stretching downward risks the parent brand's image, and judges look for that risk named alongside the volume it buys.

terms.definition: The share of the target exposed at or above the threshold number of times — conventionally three or more — so a schedule with 70% total reach may deliver only 35% of this, because the half of the audience that saw the ad once or twice does not count toward it.
terms.whyItMatters: Media-plan items give a reach curve and a frequency distribution and ask which of two schedules performs better; the one with lower total reach usually wins because more of its audience cleared the three-exposure threshold.

terms.definition: A systematic review of external conditions, competitor activity, and market trends.
terms.whyItMatters: Scanning the environment lets competitors spot opportunities and threats before deciding.

terms.definition: Time spent handling contacts and wrap-up divided by time logged in and available — 45 minutes of work inside a 50-minute available hour is 90%. Utilization puts total paid hours in the denominator instead, so it absorbs breaks, training and meetings and always reads lower; sustained occupancy above roughly 85% is the figure that predicts agent burnout.
terms.whyItMatters: A staffing roleplay judged on turnover risk needs the two denominators kept apart, or the schedule looks comfortable on paper and burns the team out.

terms.definition: The ability to discuss and reach agreements that satisfy multiple parties.
terms.whyItMatters: Negotiation determines outcomes in sales, contracts, and partnerships.

terms.definition: One percentage point of category share, worth 1% of total industry sales in dollars — $40 million in a $4 billion category. Moving from 10% to 11% share is one point but an 11% relative gain, and plans state objectives in points precisely to keep the two apart.
terms.whyItMatters: Objective-setting items ask what a stated share gain is worth in revenue, which requires multiplying the point value by industry sales rather than by the company's own sales.

terms.definition: One brand's sales to a single customer divided by that customer's total category spending over the same period — a household that spends $400 a year on coffee and $120 of it at one chain gives that chain 30% — so it is a per-customer ratio, unlike market share, which divides a brand's sales by the whole category's sales across all buyers; a brand can hold flat market share while its wallet share collapses.
terms.whyItMatters: Customer-relations roleplays that ask how to grow revenue without new customers are answered with this ratio and the cross-sell that raises it.

terms.definition: Creating a distinct name, symbol, and image for a specific offering.
terms.whyItMatters: Product branding helps customers identify and prefer that offering.

terms.definition: Unpaid media coverage generated through PR, news, and referrals.
terms.whyItMatters: Publicity builds credibility through sources other than paid ads.

terms.definition: Swapping direct identifiers for tokens while keeping the re-identification key stored separately, which leaves the file still legally personal data under GDPR Article 4(5) and still inside the regulation's reach; true anonymization destroys that key irreversibly, and only then does the data fall out of scope entirely.
terms.whyItMatters: An ethics-in-data-mining item asks whether replacing customer names with ID numbers lets a firm share the file freely, and the graded answer is that it does not while the key survives.

terms.definition: The share of paid staff time not available to take contacts — breaks, training, meetings, absence and paid leave. A center budgeting 30% shrinkage must schedule about 1.43 bodies for every agent it needs live on the phones, because 1 divided by 0.70 is 1.43; ignoring it understaffs a peak by roughly a third.
terms.whyItMatters: Peaks-in-demand roleplays ask how many people to put on the schedule, and the gross-up is where the answer is won or lost.

terms.definition: Accurately modeling what another person is thinking and feeling without necessarily sharing the feeling — perspective-taking. Affective empathy is catching the feeling itself, and compassionate empathy adds the impulse to act; only this first form can be deployed deliberately in a negotiation, and it is the one that can be trained in a session.
terms.whyItMatters: Negotiation and conflict roleplays are graded on stating the other side's reasoning back to them accurately before arguing, which is this and not sympathy.

terms.definition: The share of industry unit volume a plan must win just to cover its fixed costs: fixed costs / contribution margin per unit gives break-even units, then those units / total industry units. $2,000,000 of fixed cost at $10 contribution needs 200,000 units, which is 5% of a 4-million-unit category.
terms.whyItMatters: New-product plans are judged on whether the required share is plausible against the shares incumbents already hold; a break-even share above the category leader's is a plan a judge will reject on sight.

terms.definition: A philosophy that focuses all business activities on satisfying customer needs profitably.
terms.whyItMatters: It reminds competitors that every tactic should trace back to a real customer need.

terms.definition: Cuts slow items from a line by ranked contribution rather than by unit volume, acting on the common finding that the bottom half of a catalog produces under 5% of sales; the deciding test is what share of a cut item's buyers switch to a surviving item instead of to a rival.
terms.whyItMatters: An assortment roleplay hands you a sales-by-item list; the winning answer cuts on contribution and states the transfer assumption, because a high-volume item can carry almost no margin.

terms.definition: A schedule carrying a low continuous weight all year with heavier bursts layered over the peak selling weeks, so unlike flighting the brand is never entirely off air, and unlike continuity the weekly weight is not flat.
terms.whyItMatters: A client with year-round sales and a holiday spike is the standard prompt for this pattern; naming it and drawing the line against the other two schedules is what separates a scored answer from a vague one.

terms.definition: The European rule granting individuals rights of access, correction, portability and erasure over their own data, requiring a documented lawful basis before any processing begins, forcing breach notification to the supervisory authority within 72 hours, and capping fines at the greater of 20 million euros or 4% of worldwide annual turnover.
terms.whyItMatters: An international e-commerce roleplay asks what changes when the site starts shipping to Ireland, and the answer is these specific obligations and their clock, not a general promise of privacy.

terms.definition: Adjusting communication and approach to cultural and social differences.
terms.whyItMatters: Culturally aware service builds stronger, more diverse relationships.

terms.definition: Understanding another person's state, being moved enough to care, and then acting to help — the third mode alongside cognitive and affective empathy. It is the form that produces a commitment rather than a mirror, and because it converts feeling into action it avoids the exhaustion that pure affective empathy causes in people who absorb distress all day.
terms.whyItMatters: Judges scoring a supervisor responding to a struggling employee award the answer that names the feeling and then commits to a specific change, not the one that only shares the distress.

terms.definition: A review of a business's strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats.
terms.whyItMatters: SWOT gives a structured frame for the situation analysis behind a plan.

terms.definition: The percentage of a category's national sales occurring in one market divided by the percentage of the national population living there, multiplied by 100 — a metro holding 2% of the population but 3% of category sales scores 150 — where 100 is exactly average and anything above it means the category is over-developed in that market regardless of how any single brand performs there.
terms.whyItMatters: Media-allocation roleplays ask which markets deserve the spend; the index pair, not gut feel about city size, is what a judge expects to hear.

terms.definition: Methods such as brainstorming and focus groups used to create product concepts.
terms.whyItMatters: Structured idea generation yields higher-quality innovations.

terms.definition: The channels ads run on — TV, radio, print, digital, outdoor, and social.
terms.whyItMatters: Choosing the right media reaches the target audience cost-effectively.

terms.definition: Standards governing the responsible collection, use, protection, and sharing of information.
terms.whyItMatters: Privacy and data-governance dilemmas are common in modern business scenarios.

terms.definition: A queuing formula that converts contact volume, average handle time and a target answer speed into required agents, and its output is non-linear: doubling volume needs well under double the staff, while removing the last agent from a tight schedule can multiply wait time. Averages alone cannot produce the answer because arrivals are random, not evenly spaced.
terms.whyItMatters: Explains the counter-intuitive result in a staffing case — cutting one agent from a 20-agent schedule can break an 80/20 target outright.

terms.definition: Creating agreement and buy-in across a group with differing viewpoints.
terms.whyItMatters: It secures team alignment and commitment to shared decisions.

terms.definition: A weighted score for ranking candidate countries or segments: each factor gets a weight, the weights sum to 1.0, each market gets a rating, and weight times rating summed gives one comparable number — so a market that scores well on a 0.10 factor still loses to one that scores well on a 0.40 factor.
terms.whyItMatters: Expansion cases hand over a table of markets and ask which to enter first; the defensible answer weights the criteria before scoring rather than counting how many boxes each market ticks.

terms.definition: The bundle of benefits a business promises to deliver to a specific customer group.
terms.whyItMatters: A sharp value proposition anchors positioning, messaging, and pricing.

terms.definition: Cuts promotion, development, and service spending on a declining item toward zero while continuing to sell it, milking cash from the buyers who remain; divestment instead sells or discontinues the item outright, freeing shelf space and capital at once but ending that cash stream immediately.
terms.whyItMatters: Life-cycle roleplays put a fading item in front of you and score whether you choose between milking it and killing it, with a reason tied to remaining loyal demand.

terms.definition: Media cost divided by impressions delivered and multiplied by 1,000 — a $6,000 magazine page reaching 400,000 readers is $15 — the conversion that makes a cheap small vehicle and an expensive large one directly comparable.
terms.whyItMatters: The most common media-math item on the marketing exam gives two vehicles with different prices and different audiences and asks which is the better buy; the raw price answers nothing and this figure answers it in one step.

terms.definition: Copies only the blocks changed since the previous backup of any type, so each nightly run is the smallest possible, but restoring requires the last full backup plus every one of these runs applied in order since it — and a single missing or corrupt link breaks the entire chain behind it.
terms.whyItMatters: Records-storage items ask why a company whose nightly job finishes in four minutes still needed nine hours to recover, and the restore chain is the reason.

terms.definition: Fully loaded center cost — wages, benefits, technology and facilities — divided by contacts handled; $180,000 a month across 30,000 contacts is $6.00 each. A live phone contact typically runs several times the cost of a self-service session, and that spread, not the software licence, is the business case for deflection.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay proposing a chatbot or a help center has to set this figure against the deflected channel to justify the spend.

terms.definition: Bandura's task-specific confidence that you can carry out a particular action, built from four sources in descending order of power — a personal mastery experience, watching a similar person succeed, verbal persuasion, and how one reads one's own physical arousal. Self-esteem, by contrast, is a global judgment of personal worth, so a person can hold high esteem and low efficacy on one specific task.
terms.whyItMatters: An item asking how a manager raises a nervous employee's confidence for a first presentation wants a staged small success rather than a pep talk, since mastery outranks persuasion.

terms.definition: Dividing a market into distinct groups of customers with similar needs.
terms.whyItMatters: Segmentation lets a business target specific customer groups effectively.

terms.definition: The percentage of one brand's national sales made in a market divided by that market's percentage of national population, times 100; read against the category index it sorts markets into four actions — high BDI with low CDI means a strong brand in a weak category, while low BDI with high CDI is the classic opportunity market where the category sells well and the brand does not, and both indexes below 100 argues for withdrawal.
terms.whyItMatters: The paired index read is the standard answer to a roleplay asking which market to defend and which to invest in; giving one index without the other gets a follow-up you cannot answer.

terms.definition: Lifts a mature item's sales by changing who buys it or how often rather than changing the item: volume equals users times usage rate, so new user segments, new uses, and more use per occasion are the three levers; product modification instead alters the item's quality, features, or style.
terms.whyItMatters: Maturity-stage questions ask what a marketer does when sales flatten; the pair of levers must be told apart, since a judge hears 'add a feature' as the other strategy entirely.

terms.definition: What one rating point of a market costs: spot price divided by the program's rating, so a $3,000 spot on a 5-rated program is $600. It prices a percentage of a market where cost per thousand prices raw impressions, which is why it cannot be compared across markets of different sizes.
terms.whyItMatters: Broadcast-buying items ask a competitor to rank stations within one market, where this is the right measure, then ask to compare a small market against a large one, where it is the wrong one and cost per thousand is needed instead.

terms.definition: Copies everything changed since the last full backup, so Friday's run is far larger than Monday's, but a restore needs exactly two pieces — the full backup plus the newest run — against the incremental approach's full backup plus every intervening night in sequence.
terms.whyItMatters: A business-continuity roleplay trades nightly window against recovery speed, and the graded answer is which of these two schemes buys the shorter restore.

terms.definition: Systems and strategies for managing customer data, interactions, and relationships.
terms.whyItMatters: CRM tracks preferences and delivers personalized service at scale.

terms.term: French and Raven's five bases of power
terms.definition: Distinguishes five sources of influence — legitimate power from the position, reward power, coercive power, expert power from demonstrated knowledge, and referent power from personal respect — with the first three attached to the role and the last two to the individual. Expert and referent power produce commitment; coercive power produces compliance only while someone is watching.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay asking a new team lead with no formal authority to get cooperation is scored on building expert and referent power, and exam items on using power appropriately turn on that split.

terms.definition: (area population x annual category spending per person) / total retail selling space devoted to that category — dollars of demand per square foot of supply. A high result means demand outruns the space serving it and the trade area can carry another store; a low one means the area is already saturated.
terms.whyItMatters: Retail expansion cases hand over population, per-person spending and competitors' square footage, and the expected recommendation follows from computing this ratio rather than counting rival stores.

terms.definition: Distinct customers who bought at least once in a period divided by the total defined target population, as a percentage — 40,000 buyers out of a 500,000-person target is 8% — which counts buyers, not units or dollars; that is exactly what separates it from market share, so a brand can raise share by selling more to the same people while its penetration does not move at all.
terms.whyItMatters: Growth roleplays hinge on whether the plan should recruit new buyers or sell more to current ones, and this is the number that tells the judge you know which lever you chose.

terms.definition: Promises to repair, replace, or refund a product that fails to meet terms.
terms.whyItMatters: They reduce customer risk and signal confidence in quality.

terms.definition: Targeted messages sent straight to individuals by mail, email, or phone.
terms.whyItMatters: Direct marketing allows personalized, measurable, one-to-one engagement.

terms.definition: The mathematical examination of data to identify patterns, test relationships, and support decisions.
terms.whyItMatters: Competitors are tested on interpreting findings and drawing evidence-based conclusions.

terms.definition: Closed cases a customer reopens divided by cases closed in the period — 60 of 1,200 is 5%. It is the audit on first contact resolution: an agent can inflate the resolution figure by closing tickets early, and this is the only metric that catches it, which is why the two are always reported as a pair.
terms.whyItMatters: In a service-quality case, the competitor who pairs a resolution claim with this check shows the judge they know the headline metric can be gamed.

terms.definition: Leading by modeling integrity, fairness, and moral principles.
terms.whyItMatters: It builds organizational trust and sets the tone for employee behavior.

terms.definition: Forecast accuracy scored as the average of |actual minus forecast| / actual across periods — a +10% miss and a -10% miss do not cancel, because the absolute value is taken before averaging. That is exactly what separates it from forecast bias, which keeps the signs.
terms.whyItMatters: Sales-forecasting items give several months of forecast and actual pairs and ask how accurate the method was; averaging the signed errors returns a flattering near-zero that the item is designed to catch.

terms.definition: The core marketing activities such as pricing, promotion, selling, and distribution.
terms.whyItMatters: Competitors organize their analysis around which marketing functions a decision touches.

terms.definition: Puts a written or drawn description of an unbuilt product before target buyers and scores stated purchase intent, normally reading the top two boxes of a 5-point scale -- 'definitely' plus 'probably would buy' -- then discounting that figure, because stated intent runs far above actual trial.
terms.whyItMatters: Feasibility roleplays ask how you would test an idea before building it; naming the intent scale and the discount separates a real answer from 'ask some customers.'

terms.definition: Total media spend divided by completed conversions rather than by clicks — $800 producing 16 purchases is $50, even though that same $800 buying 3,200 clicks made cost per click look like $0.25. Rising here with a flat cost per click means the landing page, not the media, is failing.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam item showing cheap clicks and expensive customers is testing whether the competitor can locate the failure downstream of the ad, and a roleplay client who wants to cut the ad budget is usually the one who needs the page fixed.

terms.definition: A 99.999% uptime commitment, which permits roughly 5.3 minutes of unplanned downtime across an entire year; each nine dropped multiplies that allowance by ten, so 99.99% permits about 53 minutes, 99.9% about 8.8 hours, and 99% about 3.65 days — which is why a vendor's extra decimal costs so much.
terms.whyItMatters: A vendor-selection roleplay compares two hosting quotes whose uptime promises differ by one decimal, and converting each into annual minutes is what makes the price gap defensible.

terms.definition: The clock from a customer's message to the first substantive human reply, which stops on that reply even though nothing is fixed yet; resolution time runs on until the issue is actually closed. A 1-hour response with a 3-day resolution is a legitimate and common pair, and quoting one figure for both makes a team look twice as fast as it is.
terms.whyItMatters: Email and social-service roleplays set two separate targets, so a competitor who reports a single number has misread the case.

terms.definition: Models trustworthiness as credibility plus reliability plus intimacy, all divided by self-orientation — so visibly acting in your own interest divides away everything the other three terms earn. Credibility is about words, reliability about repeated actions over time, and intimacy about safety in disclosure, which is why a person can be believable and still not be trusted.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay on rebuilding a client or coworker relationship is scored on lowering the self-orientation term — leading with their problem — rather than on producing more credentials.

terms.definition: A projection of expected future sales based on analysis and historical data.
terms.whyItMatters: Forecasts help plan resources and set realistic marketing objectives.

terms.definition: The top rung of the three-stage loyalty ladder: at recognition the buyer merely knows the mark, at preference the buyer chooses it but accepts a substitute when it is out of stock, and at insistence the buyer will leave the store or delay the purchase rather than take another brand — the only stage that lets a firm hold price through a competitor's promotion.
terms.whyItMatters: Branding roleplays ask what a strong brand is actually worth; naming the three stages and the out-of-stock behavior that separates preference from insistence is what earns the point.

terms.definition: Laws and rules ensuring fair practices and safeguarding customer rights.
terms.whyItMatters: Understanding it helps a business operate ethically and avoid liability.

terms.definition: Customer recommendations and referrals that spread opinions about a product.
terms.whyItMatters: Word-of-mouth builds organic advocacy and trust beyond paid ads.

terms.definition: A cloud arrangement where the provider runs the hardware, storage and virtualization while the customer still patches the operating system and everything stacked above it; platform services shift that operating system and runtime to the provider, and software as a service leaves the customer responsible for nothing but their own data and user settings.
terms.whyItMatters: A technology-impact item asks who is at fault when an unpatched server is breached, and the answer depends entirely on which of these three lines the contract drew.

terms.definition: Contacts passed up to a supervisor or a higher support tier divided by total contacts. A transfer moves a contact sideways to a peer queue; an escalation moves it up a level of authority — so an agent whose refund limit is $50 must escalate every $60 refund, and the rate is measuring the policy, not the customers.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays about empowering frontline staff turn on this: raising an agent's approval limit is usually the cheapest way to cut it.

terms.definition: The work of managing your own feelings to satisfy an employer's display rules — the face the job requires — and it is performed two ways: surface acting, which puts on the expression while the underlying feeling is unchanged, and deep acting, which alters the felt emotion itself. Surface acting is the strategy repeatedly tied to higher exhaustion and turnover; deep acting is not.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay on staffing a long shift of difficult interactions is scored on recognizing that requiring a constant smile is a real cost to be scheduled around, not a free instruction.

terms.definition: Next period's forecast equals alpha times this period's actual plus (1 minus alpha) times this period's forecast, with alpha between 0 and 1. A high alpha makes the forecast chase recent movement; a low alpha holds it steady, and every past period stays in the number at a shrinking weight.
terms.whyItMatters: Forecasting questions give last period's forecast, its actual and a smoothing constant and expect one number back; they also ask which alpha suits a volatile category, which is a judgment the formula makes visible.

terms.definition: The added value a strong, well-known brand name gives a product.
terms.whyItMatters: Brand equity explains why customers pay more for, and stay loyal to, established brands.

terms.definition: A pre-release trial run by the developer's own employees inside a controlled company setting, so defects are found before any outsider sees the product; beta testing hands the same build to real customers in their own environment, which makes who runs it and where the dividing line between the two.
terms.whyItMatters: Development-stage exam items list a testing activity and ask which stage it belongs to; the answer turns entirely on whether outsiders are involved.

terms.definition: Revenue attributable to a campaign divided by what that campaign cost: $40,000 of revenue on $10,000 of spend is 4.0. It differs from return on investment, which subtracts cost of goods and the spend itself before dividing, so a 4.0 here is still a losing campaign at a 20% gross margin.
terms.whyItMatters: A client presenting a campaign as a four-to-one success is the setup for this distinction; the competitor is expected to ask for the margin before agreeing the campaign made money.

terms.definition: The computational discovery of patterns and correlations hidden in large datasets.
terms.whyItMatters: Mining surfaces competitive insights that simple reports would miss.

terms.definition: Help-center or bot sessions that end without a human contact, divided by total sessions — 7,000 of 10,000 is 70%. A session only counts as deflected when no contact follows inside a set window, usually 24 hours; without that window an abandoned bot session where the customer gave up and phoned later is scored as a save.
terms.whyItMatters: The savings claim in a technology-in-CRM roleplay collapses without the follow-up window, and judges look for the competitor who states it.

terms.definition: Fisher and Ury's method built on four rules — separate the people from the problem, focus on interests instead of stated positions, invent options for mutual gain before deciding anything, and insist on an objective standard for the outcome. A position is what a party demands; the interest is why they want it, and only the interest can usually be satisfied in more than one way.
terms.whyItMatters: Negotiation roleplays are scored on surfacing the reason behind a demand and offering two options that meet it, which positional haggling over one number cannot produce.

terms.definition: Among households that buy the brand at all, the percentage of their category purchases it captures. A brand bought by 20% of households that supplies 60% of those households' category volume has 60% share of requirements but only 12% market share (0.20 x 0.60).
terms.whyItMatters: Growth-diagnosis items ask whether a brand should recruit new buyers or deepen existing ones; a high requirements share with low penetration points to recruitment, and the two numbers must be read together.

terms.definition: Attributes a brand must match well enough for buyers to accept it as a legitimate member of the category — a car that is safe, a bank that clears deposits — which buy entry and win no preference at all; the attributes that win preference are points of difference, and because parity is a threshold rather than a scale, money spent beating a rival on a parity attribute returns nothing.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay asking where to invest a product-improvement budget is a parity-versus-difference question; spending to over-deliver on a category minimum is the error the judge is watching for.

terms.definition: The specific benefit that makes a product distinctly better than rivals'.
terms.whyItMatters: A clear USP gives customers a compelling reason to choose the product.

terms.definition: An ad's key elements — headline, copy, visuals, call to action, and branding.
terms.whyItMatters: Each component ensures the ad communicates its message persuasively.

terms.definition: The final digit of a code such as a twelve-digit UPC, computed from the digits before it so a scanner can catch its own misread: multiply the digits in odd positions by three, add the digits in even positions, and choose the last digit that lifts the total to the next multiple of ten.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-records questions ask how a scanner knows a keyed-in barcode was mistyped without any lookup, and this arithmetic is the mechanism.

terms.definition: A grid that derives a case's priority from how many people or how much revenue is affected, set against how fast the situation degrades — high impact with high urgency becomes P1, high impact with low urgency P2, and so on across a 3x3 or 4x4 grid. Priority is computed from the two axes rather than argued by whoever complains loudest.
terms.whyItMatters: Given a backlog of angry customers in a roleplay, the competitor who sorts by this grid instead of by volume of complaint wins the judged point on fairness.

terms.definition: Short for best alternative to a negotiated agreement: the course of action you would actually take if these talks failed, which is what sets real bargaining power. It is not the price target and not the reservation price — the reservation price is the worst deal still worth accepting, derived from the alternative — and improving the outside option raises your power even if nothing at the table changes.
terms.whyItMatters: A supplier or salary negotiation roleplay is scored on the candidate knowing their walk-away option and estimating the other side's before conceding.

terms.definition: A specific, measurable goal for what marketing should achieve.
terms.whyItMatters: Clear objectives keep strategies and tactics aligned with business goals.

terms.definition: Attributes buyers strongly associate with one brand, rate favorably, and believe no competitor delivers as well — all three conditions, not just the first — which is what makes them the reason to choose it, unlike points of parity, which only qualify the brand for the consideration set; once rivals match a claimed difference it has quietly become a parity attribute and stops moving share even though the advertising still runs.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked to identify what sets a company apart, a competitor who names a feature every rival also offers has named a parity attribute and will be corrected on the spot.

terms.definition: The first 2.5% of a market to buy something new -- venturesome, able to absorb a failed purchase, and often socially outside the mainstream, which limits their influence; the early adopters who follow are the next 13.5% and carry the opinion leadership that actually moves the majority.
terms.whyItMatters: New-product roleplays ask who to target at launch; quoting the 2.5% band and then explaining why that group cannot spread adoption alone is what separates the top scores.

terms.definition: An auction in which the winner pays one increment above the runner-up's bid rather than the amount they themselves bid, so a $4.00 bid beating a $2.50 bid clears at $2.51 — which is why bidding true value can never cost more than that value is worth.
terms.whyItMatters: Digital-buying items ask why an advertiser should enter its real maximum instead of shading the bid down; the mechanic, not the strategy, is the answer, and competitors who guess pay-what-you-bid get it backwards.

terms.definition: Normalization's opening stage: every column holds one indivisible value and no table repeats a group of columns across a single row (no phone1, phone2, phone3). It removes repeating groups and nothing else — a partial dependency on part of a composite key survives it, and a transitive dependency survives both it and the second stage.
terms.whyItMatters: A database item hands the competitor a customer table with three comma-packed phone columns and asks which normal form it breaks; the answer is the first, and answering the third throws the point away.

terms.definition: A total outage or safety-affecting failure with no workaround, carrying the tightest published clock — commonly a 15-minute acknowledgement, hourly status updates and continuous work until restoration. Severity rates the technical damage while priority adds business context, so a Sev-1 affecting one tiny account can still be worked at P2.
terms.whyItMatters: Service-level roleplays hinge on the severity-versus-priority split, and quoting the acknowledgement clock is what makes the answer specific rather than reassuring.

terms.definition: Over-weighting a person's character and under-weighting their circumstances when explaining someone else's behavior — the late colleague is careless rather than stuck behind an accident. Its mirror image applied to oneself is the self-serving bias, and together the pair make an appraisal reward good luck and punish bad context.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam item asking why a supervisor rates a rep poorly after a territory loses its largest account expects this bias by name, and roleplays on fair evaluation reward asking about conditions before judging the person.

terms.definition: Revenue times percent margin, minus marketing and sales expense: $10,000,000 at a 40% margin spending $2,500,000 contributes $1,500,000. Unlike marketing ROI it reports dollars added rather than a ratio, so a small program with a spectacular ratio can still contribute less than a large one.
terms.whyItMatters: Plan-defense questions ask which of two programs to fund when one has the better return percentage and the other the bigger dollar contribution; the profit line is settled in dollars.

terms.definition: The percentage of total sales in a market captured by one business or product.
terms.whyItMatters: Market share quantifies competitive position and the payoff of a growth strategy.

terms.definition: The 13.5% of buyers who follow the innovators -- respected opinion leaders inside the mainstream whose endorsement decides whether an item reaches the 34% early majority; innovators, the first 2.5%, buy sooner but sit too far outside the group to persuade it.
terms.whyItMatters: Promotion plans for a launch are scored on targeting the group that others watch; naming the 13.5% band and its opinion-leader role answers the indicator directly.

terms.definition: Coordinating all promotion for one consistent message across channels.
terms.whyItMatters: Consistency across touchpoints reinforces the message and maximizes impact.

terms.definition: A structured request that filters and retrieves specific information from a database.
terms.whyItMatters: Querying lets competitors pull exactly the data they need instead of sifting everything.

terms.definition: The contractual penalty owed when a provider misses its service-level target — typically 10% of the monthly fee for the first missed tier, rising by band and capped at 100%. In most agreements it is the customer's sole remedy, and it must be claimed inside a stated window, often 30 days, or the right to it lapses entirely.
terms.whyItMatters: In a business-to-business account roleplay, the competitor who knows the credit must be requested rather than issued automatically recovers real money for the client.
